role: Script of 2026-11-13 that built bw_old and bw_new and ran the first test.
purpose: `run_kernels.sh` compiles the old benchmark source `bandwidth.orig.c` into the binary `bw_old` and the new source `bandwidth.c` into `bw_new`, writes the machine code of every kernel to `probe.txt`, and runs a self-test. In mode `all` it then times every kernel of both binaries, first with 1 thread and then with 120 threads on CPUs 0 to 119.

main_flow.step: Set the shell options that stop the script at a failed command and at an unset variable. Then restart the script under `taskset -c 0-119`. The script and every process that it starts may then use CPUs 0 to 119 only.
Read the mode (`probe` or `all`). Stop if the marker file exists.
Find the script folder and create the result folder `kernels-TIME` (`TIME` is the UTC time).
Set the compiler flags. Write host, time, load averages, gcc version and flags to `probe.txt`.
Build `bw_old`, `bw_new`, `selftest` and `probe.o` with the same flags. Stop if a build fails.
Append the checksums of sources and binaries and the machine code of the six kernels of each binary to `probe.txt`.
Run the self-test. Stop with status 4 if it fails.
Mode `all`: run 192 processes with 1 thread each, on CPU 0 and on CPU 2, with four buffer sizes. Their rows go to `one-thread.csv`.
Mode `all`: run 24 processes with 120 threads each. Their rows go to `threads120.csv`. This is the part that ra.sh repeats.
Append the load averages after the last process to `probe.txt` and print the result folder.

behavior_notes: The rerun of 2026-11-17 did not start this script. go.sh calls ra.sh, and ra.sh uses the binaries `bw_old` and `bw_new` that this script built on CRB on 2026-11-13 [Ref8].

Every start of the script builds the binaries again. Three result folders of this script exist from 2026-11-13. Their starts were at 18:12:10 UTC (mode `probe`) [Ref4], at 18:12:22 UTC (mode `all`) [Ref1] and at 18:32:18 UTC (mode `probe`) [Ref5]. All three `probe.txt` files record the same sha256 for `bw_old` (e8fc0205...) and the same sha256 for `bw_new` (fd7c14df...) [Ref1] [Ref4] [Ref5]. ra.sh checks these two values [Ref8].

The new source changed between the starts. `bandwidth.c` had the sha256 c1406e02... at 18:12:10 UTC and at 18:12:22 UTC, and f1985072... at 18:32:18 UTC [Ref4] [Ref1] [Ref5]. The sha256 of `bw_new` and the machine code of the kernels in `probe.txt` did not change [Ref1] [Ref5]. The local `bandwidth.c` has the sha256 f1985072... [Ref3]. The two texts differ in comment lines only. An edit of 2026-11-13 18:32:07 UTC replaced 2 comment lines above `k_read` with the 5 comment lines 178 to 182 of the local text [Ref14]. With this edit reversed, the local text has the sha256 value of the earlier text (c1406e02...). No code line differs.

Compiler result for the read kernels, from the listing [Ref1]: gcc turned the 16 sums of the old `k_read` into 8 vector registers with 2 sums each. One loop pass of the old `k_read` in `bw_old` has 4 `ldp q` loads (128 bytes) and 8 vector `add` instructions that add the loaded values to the sums. One loop pass of the new `k_read` in `bw_new` has 8 `ldp q` loads (256 bytes) and no instruction that uses the loaded values.

Compiler result for the instruction sets, from the listing [Ref1]: the old `k_write` and `k_copy` in `bw_old` use SVE instructions (`whilelo`, `st1d`, `ld1d`). `-march=native` is the only flag of line 19 that sets the target architecture. The architecture decides which instructions gcc may use [Ref12]. A record from CRB of 2026-11-11 shows what the same gcc version picked for `native`: the architecture name `armv8-a` with 16 extensions (sets of extra instructions), among them four SVE2 extensions [Ref13]. The ten other kernel listings of the two binaries hold no SVE instruction.

Compiler result for `-fno-tree-loop-distribute-patterns`, from the listing [Ref1]: no kernel calls `memset` or `memcpy`. The only call in the twelve kernel listings is the stack check of the old `k_read`.

The old `k_read` in `bw_old` ends with a call to `__stack_chk_fail`, which belongs to a stack check. The instructions of the check sit before and after the loop, not inside it [Ref1]. No flag of line 19 asks for it. Insufficient data: the options that the gcc of CRB turns on without a flag. The output of `gcc -v` and of `gcc -Q --help=common -O3 -march=native` on CRB would resolve it.

Source of the flag meanings on line 19: the help text of the local gcc 11.4.0 for x86-64 [Ref9]. The meaning of `-march=native` on an Arm machine comes from the public manual of gcc 14.2.0 [Ref12]. The value that gcc picked for `native` on CRB comes from a record of 2026-11-11, two days before the build [Ref13]. The `probe.txt` files of 2026-11-13 do not record this value. No manual page of gcc is installed on the local machine. CRB used gcc 14.2.0 [Ref1]. Insufficient data: the exact list of steps that `-O3` turns on in gcc 14.2.0 on CRB. The output of `gcc -Q --help=optimizers -O3` on CRB would resolve it.

The self-test covers the new source only. `selftest.c` includes `bandwidth.c` [Ref6]. It does not check the kernels `read`, `write` and `copy` of the old source `bandwidth.orig.c`. The three hand-written kernels have the same source text in both files [Ref3].

Order of the processes: one process holds one kernel of one binary. So no kernel is timed after another kernel in the same process. But the processes follow each other without a wait. On 2026-11-13 the 1-minute load average was 1.00 at the first 120-thread process and 85.38 at the last one [Ref2].

What one 120-thread process does [Ref3]: each thread first pins itself to one CPU (thread number i to CPU i). Then it allocates its own buffer of 256 MiB, asks Linux for huge pages for it, and writes it once before any timing. It writes with `k_write`, the function of the kernel `write` of the same binary. For `copy` and `asmcopy` each thread has a second buffer of the same size. Before each of the 3 intervals every thread runs the kernel once over its buffer without timing. Then all threads start together. In each of the 3 intervals a thread reads the clock at its start and after each whole pass over its buffer. It stops when 0.5 s or more have passed.

The rate [Ref3]: the binary prints one row per interval. Per pass over its buffer a thread counts the size of the buffer in bytes. For `copy` and `asmcopy` it counts twice that size: the bytes that it read plus the bytes that it wrote. The column `aggregate_GBps` is the sum of the bytes of all threads, divided by the longest elapsed time of any thread, in GB/s. Each process also prints a comment line, a title line and one `best` row with the highest of its 3 rates.
The marker file is checked at the start, before the self-test and before each benchmark process. Nothing checks it while a process runs.

The script can stop early. Status 2: unknown mode. Status 3: the marker file exists. Status 5: a build failed. Status 4: the self-test failed. A benchmark process that fails stops the script with its own status. Mode `probe` ends with status 0 after the self-test.

The local file is the script that ran. Its sha256 (6a91bbbe...) equals the value that all three `probe.txt` files record [Ref1] [Ref4] [Ref5]. The local files `bandwidth.orig.c` (61228754...), `selftest.c` (90456a56...) and `probe.c` (81f96b39...) also have the sha256 values that all three files record [Ref1] [Ref4] [Ref5].

The binaries `bw_old` and `bw_new` are not in the local folders. Their sha256 values are known only from records such as the three `probe.txt` files of this script [Ref1] [Ref4] [Ref5] and the two values that ra.sh checks [Ref8].

words.def: the Arm reference server under test. It has 128 CPUs.
the two halves of the chip. CPUs 0-63 sit on mesh 0. CPUs 64-127 sit on mesh 1.
our runs use CPUs 0-119 only: 64 threads on mesh 0 plus 56 threads on mesh 1. Each thread reads its own buffer of 256 MiB from memory.
the inner loop of the benchmark that reads memory. On this page "kernel" means this loop. The operating system kernel is always written "Linux kernel".
portable C code with 16 running sums. Each load is followed by an add. Its name is `read` in the binary bw_old and `oldread` in the runner bwx12.
NEON intrinsics (C functions that map to Arm vector instructions), loads only. Its name is `read` in the binary bw_new and `read` in bwx12.
a hand-written load-only loop. It has the same 8 "ldp q" loads per 256 B as the new read kernel. "ldp q" is the Arm instruction that loads two 16-byte vector registers.

the four other kernels of bw_old and bw_new. `write` fills a buffer. `copy` copies one buffer to a second buffer. `asmwrite` and `asmcopy` are hand-written loops for the same two jobs. They are not read kernels.
the benchmark and its two binaries of 2026-11-13. bw_old was built from the old source, bw_new from the new source.
later runner programs for the same loops. They print one row per thread. bwx12 is the runner of the 2026-11-15 investigation. bwx11 and bwx are older versions.

a process is one start of a benchmark binary. An interval is one timed measurement inside a process. bwx12 times a sequence of kernels and repeats the sequence: each repeat is a round (counted from 0), and the position is the place of a kernel in the sequence (counted from 0). In part A the round (1 or 2) is the round of the script: round 2 runs the processes in the reverse order.
the 120-thread part of the test of 2026-11-13, repeated with the same two binaries.
the script of the rerun of 2026-11-17 that runs part A. It uses the binaries that run_kernels.sh built.
the driver script of the rerun of 2026-11-17. It calls ra.sh.
an analysis script that reads threads120.csv.
the GNU C compiler.
a tool that prints the machine code of a binary as assembler text.
the instructions that the compiler produced for a function. The listing is their text form in probe.txt.
one execution of the body of a loop.
the Arm vector instructions with 16-byte registers. The listing writes these registers as `q` or `v` with a number.
the Scalable Vector Extension, another set of Arm vector instructions. The listing writes its registers as `z` or `p` with a number.

the Scalable Vector Extension 2, a further set of Arm vector instructions. The record of 2026-11-11 names four SVE2 extensions [Ref13]. The gcc manual says that each of them also turns on SVE2, and that SVE2 also turns on the SVE instructions [Ref12].

code that the compiler adds to a function. At entry the function copies a guard value to its stack frame. Before it returns it compares the copy with the guard value. On a difference it calls `__stack_chk_fail`.
the program `selftest`. It checks what the kernels do to memory. Exit status 0 means that every check passed.
`/tmp/positron-perf.RUNNING`. Another user creates it during a performance test [Ref11]. Our scripts stop when it exists.

the number of tasks that are runnable or wait for disk input and output, averaged by Linux over the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes (file /proc/loadavg). The fourth field of the file gives the tasks that are runnable now and the number of all tasks.

the column pcpu of the tool ps. It is the CPU time that a process has used, divided by the time since the process started. So it is an average over the life of the process. It is not the use at the moment of the reading.
a checksum. Two files with the same sha256 have the same content.
memory pages of 2 MiB that Linux can use for a buffer in place of its smaller standard pages.
a thread that is pinned to a CPU may run on that CPU only.
GB = 1e9 bytes. KiB = 2^10 bytes, MiB = 2^20 bytes, GiB = 2^30 bytes. The size arguments `32K`, `1M`, `8M`, `256M` and `1G` use the binary units: `256M` means 256 MiB = 268435456 bytes.
the number that a program returns when it ends. 0 means success.
Coordinated Universal Time. The scripts write every time in UTC.
a Linux tool that starts a command with a limit on the CPUs that the command may use.

external source: manual of gcc 14.2.0, page "AArch64 Options", entry `-march=name`, read on 2026-11-21. The entry says that the value `native` "causes the compiler to pick the architecture of the host system". It says that gcc uses the architecture name to decide which instructions it can emit. It also says that with `-march` and without `-mtune` or `-mcpu` the code is tuned for a range of processors that implement the architecture. The sub-section "-march and -mcpu Feature Modifiers" of the same page says that each of `sve2-aes`, `sve2-bitperm`, `sve2-sha3` and `sve2-sm4` also enables SVE2 instructions, and that `sve2` also enables SVE instructions.

A record from CRB of 2026-11-11 at 21:00:17 UTC. Line 4 holds the same gcc version text as line 2 of Ref1. Line 5 holds what `gcc -march=native -Q --help=target` printed for the options `-march=`, `-mcpu=` and `-mtune=`. The value of `-march=` is `armv8-a` with 16 extensions. Four of them are SVE2 extensions: `sve2-aes`, `sve2-bitperm`, `sve2-sha3` and `sve2-sm4`. The values of `-mcpu=` and `-mtune=` are empty. The file probe-20261111T210017Z.cmd.txt in the same folder holds the commands that wrote the record.
